Read more A t 6:29am on 7 October 2023, Mia Schem was filming a video with her friend Elia Toledano when the sound of rockets started. They had been waiting for the sun to rise over the Negev desert in southern Israel at the Nova music festival, just 3 miles from the Israel- Gaza border. By the end of the day, the 21-year-old describes how she was shot in the arm by a Hamas militant and taken hostage into the Gaza Strip, and 378 people from the festival would be among 1,200 people killed. Israel launched a relentless two-year barrage of strikes in response, leaving 70,000 Palestinians dead in Gaza and reducing much of the enclave to rubble. In the early days of the war, Hamas released a video of Schem in captivity , the first footage of any of the 251 hostages. The French- Israeli citizen was held in Gaza for 55 days before being released during a brief truce between Israel and Hamas. open image in gallery Mia Schem, 21, appears in a Hamas hostage video in the days following the 7 October attacks. ( AFP/Hamas handout ) Speaking with The Independent in London, Schem has flown from her home in Shoham, a town on the outskirts of Tel Aviv in Israel. She said she had only decided to attend the music festival on a whim. “I remember that I asked Elia, ‘Do you want to go to the Nova Festival?’ and he tell me ‘Yes, why not?’” she says. She drove to Toledano’s house, her best friend, and they took his car to the festival site. “I didn’t know the party was close to Gaza,” she says, because the organisers of the Nova festival tended to share the locations of the raves only a few hours before the scheduled start time. Even if she had known that information, it would not have impacted her decision to go. “Who thought that something like that would happen,” she says. open image in gallery Palestinian militants move towards the border fence with Israel from Khan Yunis in the southern Gaza Strip on October 7, 2023. ( AFP via Getty Images ) Once the rockets started, Schem grabbed Toledano and headed straight for his car. She believes they were one of the first few cars to leave the Nova festival site. At this stage in the day seemingly innocuous decisions would decide whether or not you would survive the terrorist attack. When leaving the festival site those who turned right were saved, Schem says, and those who turned left towards Tel Aviv and Jerusalem were met by Hamas. “Me and Elia were the first people to see the terrorists,” she says. Hamas gunmen were standing at either side of the road, shooting at cars and killing passengers as they sped past. Schem thought there could have been as many as 40 gunmen in the road. Schem floored it through the roadblock but says their car was riddled with bullets. open image in gallery Abandoned vehicles at the site of the 7 October attack on the Nova music festival in the Negev desert in southern Israel. ( AFP via Getty Images ) The vehicle rolled twice, and Toledano and Schem were forced to escape out of the vehicle’s windows, as the doors were jammed. They tried to hide next to the car. Toledano grabbed her phone and began calling the emergency services, but the messages that came back were grim. “They tell us on the phone, ‘You need to hide. We can’t help you,’” Schem says, “Nobody came to save us.” When she was hiding on the ground, she was shot in the arm by a Hamas terrorist: “ They shot me from point-blank range.” Both Schem and Toledano were abducted and taken into Gaza. Only one of them would return alive. The body of Elia Toledano would be eventually retrieved by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) from the Gaza Strip in late 2023. There was a “ high probability ” that his cause of death was due to an Israeli airstrike, according to an IDF investigation. open image in gallery Palestinian militants transport a reportedly captured Israeli woman by motorcycle, in Khan Yunis in the southern Gaza Strip. ( AFP via Getty Images ) When describing her time in Hamas captivity in Gaza, Schem is unequivocal. She was treated like an “animal in a cage,” she recounts. She believes the only reason she was saved from being raped was because she was being kept in the home of her captor. “He didn’t touch me, but the reason was because his wife and children were behind the door,” Schem adds. She said her captor’s wife would mistreat Schem because she resented the fact that she was in the same room as her husband: “She didn’t give me water or food.” Five days before she was released, Schem says she was taken down into the tunnels beneath Gaza where she first encountered other hostages.Five women were also being held there. Schem has told Israeli television that this was the hardest time of her captivity because of the hopelessness of the hostages she met down there. open image in gallery Visitors walk among burnt out cars and tents at the Nova Music Festival Exhibition in Berlin, Germany. ( Getty Images ) Schem was in London to recount her story to an audience at the Nova Exhibition. The exhibition recreates the music festival with real wreckage brought over from Israel. “ It's a miracle that I'm here.” she says, “and if God saved me, I never give up.” The exhibition has been travelling around the world, and London is the 10th city it has visited so far. Now, plans are underway for the exhibition to travel to Paris, Budapest and Prague in the future. When the exhibition travelled to New York, hundreds of people gathered in Lower Manhattan to protest against Israel’s conduct since October 7th, with some accusing the show of being political propaganda. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/14/migra.text: A plane operated by non-governmental organisations assisting migrants in the Mediterranean spotted 11 decomposing bodies in the sea off the coast of Libya on Friday.The SOS Méditerranée NGO called it a "harrowing scene" in a statement, saying "some of the bodies still had clothes on, others were kept afloat by tire inner tubes".It said the bodies were "in an advanced state of decomposition.""This sighting is a stark reminder of the human consequences of Europe's deadly policies of indifference and deterrence-at-all-costs," the organisation said in a statement.The Italian coast guard said it had been notified and had informed Libyan authorities since the bodies were in Libya's search and rescue zone.It said the bodies were around 57 nautical miles (105 kilometres) from the Libyan coastal city of Zuwarah.The monitoring plane was operated by SOS Méditerranée and the Humanitarian Pilots Initiative.Every year, tens of thousands of migrants attempt to cross the sea from north Africa to southern member states of the European Union.The International Organisation for Migration said this week that the number of known migrant deaths in the central Mediterranean has increased drastically, even as migrant numbers fall because of harsher European policies.It said 821 people died or went missing in the first four months of 2026, a 111% increase from 2025. More than half of the deaths were caused by severe weather in January.Over the same period, migrant arrivals on that route fell by 46% to 8,577.The EU border agency Frontex said the total number of irregular border crossings into the European Union fell by 26% in 2025 from the previous year to almost 178,000.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g.text: Figure caption, Watch: The documents that were falsified to allow Roman Abramovich to evade tax By James Oliver ,Â Rory Tinman ,Â BBC Panorama ,Â Harriet Agerholm ,Â BBC Verify Â and Â Simon Lock ,Â the Bureau of Investigative Journalism Published 12 October 2026 The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found. Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (Â£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts. Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents. Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant". Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals. Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws". The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism. For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club. Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, Â£5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years. The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes". Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Chateau de la Croe (top left) in the south of France, Fyning Hill in Sussex and two superyachts vanished from company accounts The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022. The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism , external - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential , external investigation. In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false. The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city. Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune. The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices. Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune He was the Russian oligarch who brought his wealth to the UK. But whatâs the truth about Roman Abramovichâs fortune? Panorama investigates the documents that were falsified to hide his wealth and evade tax. Watch on iPlayer Watch now on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST on Monday 12 October. Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth. Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property. A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus. Image caption, Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history. They drew up a plan to circumvent the transparency law by transferring the assets to Amiscan's parent company in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), where they could be kept hidden. And they backdated the change by three years to make it look like the asset transfer had happened in 2003. Deloitte Cyprus reviewed the backdated documents and said they were "adequate" to allow them to remove the assets from Amiscan's accounts. When the 2003 accounts were signed off by Deloitte in 2006, the homes, planes and yachts disappeared at the stroke of a pen. Only $75,000 of assets remained. Deloitte signed off the accounts even though the leaked documents show it knew they were completely misleading. Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts. Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme. This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003. It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities. But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history. Abramovich's close associate misled UK court in Â£1bn oil-fields case, documents suggest An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read. MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money. A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree". MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI. This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus. Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets. So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax. Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said. Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law." In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus. MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune. It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public. Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier. MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000. Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear. Andrew Mitchell KC told Panorama: "What you take away from it is there are professionals who are prepared to bend and break the rules of their profession and therefore the law. And it looks that they will stop literally at nothing in terms of creating documents." Vladimir Milov, Russia's deputy minister of energy as Abramovich built his empire and now a critic of the Russian government, said: "For each Russian oligarch or Middle Eastern or African corrupt oligarch, there's an army of Western financial and legal services and PR services providers, who is easily taking money for whitewashing their reputation and making them look normal." Denying any wrongdoing by the oligarch, Roman Abramovich's lawyers said that he was "not involved in the day-to-day operation of those companies" and that where arrangements were proposed by professional advisers, "reliance on that advice was entirely proper and legitimate". Deloitte Cyprus said it could not comment on the specific allegations because the documents were more than 20 years old and no longer accessible. MeritServus closed following the Cyprus Confidential leak. Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here. https://english.radio.cz/bone-glue-devel.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Bone glue developed by Brno scientists could help treat complex fractures Facebook Twitter Bone glue developed by Brno scientists could help treat complex fractures 3:08 ⨯ Bone glue developed by Brno scientists could help treat complex fractures https://english.radio.cz/bone-glue-developed-brno-scientists-could-help-treat-complex-fractures-8898568#player=on Copy Share on social media Facebook X Scientists in Brno have developed a special bone glue that could one day help doctors treat even complicated fractures. The material is now being tested on sheep. The special bone glue was developed at the CEITEC research centre at Brno University of Technology, together with surgeons from Brno University Hospital and Masaryk University. Using sheep, researchers are testing whether it can help repair broken bones and eventually be absorbed by the body. Surgeon Milan Krtička from Brno University Hospital describes how the glue is being tested: “We are creating a hole in the middle of the metacarpal bone. We drill out a small piece of bone so that we can test the glue, and then glue the piece back into place. We will see how the glue attaches to the bone, becomes integrated and eventually turns into new bone.” While the surgeons prepare the bone, researchers have to mix the glue very quickly so that it does not harden too soon. Once it hardens, the material becomes porous and helps new bone to form, says Lenka Michlovská, a scientist at CEITEC. The glue could eventually be used for complicated fractures in which a bone breaks into several pieces. Michlovská explains why the way it is applied could be particularly useful: “The advantage is that it can be applied with a syringe, for example under X-ray guidance. That means the whole fracture would not necessarily have to be opened up.” The new material could also overcome a limitation of existing bone adhesives. Methacrylate adhesives are mainly used to bond bone to metal in implants, rather than to join broken bone fragments. Krtička says one of the main innovations is that the new glue is designed to work even when there is blood around the injured bone: “None of the adhesives tested so far have been tested in this kind of living, bloody environment. They were tested completely dry. The innovation here is that, thanks to the adhesive bridge, this glue will have the ability to attach to the bone even when there is blood present.” First, the researchers apply an adhesive bridge to help the glue attach to the bone, rather like a primer before painting, and only then apply the bone glue. Krtička describes what happens next: “It is a kind of ceramic paste. I apply it with a syringe to the site I have prepared, where I drilled out the piece of bone, and then I glue the piece back into place. We close the wound, and the experimental operation is over.” The sheep will be monitored for several weeks to see how well the bones heal and how the glue behaves in the body. If the results are promising, the researchers will carry out further tests before the material could eventually be considered for use in human medicine. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Barack Obama arrives at a campaign rally at Cass Technical high school on Saturday. Photograph: Paul Sancya/AP View image in fullscreen Barack Obama arrives at a campaign rally at Cass Technical high school on Saturday. Photograph: Paul Sancya/AP Michigan Obama rallies rapturous Michigan crowd for El-Sayed: ‘He’ll finish the job we started’ Former president speaks to crowd of thousands in support of Abdul El-Sayed for US Senate and Democratic ticket Joseph Gedeon in Detroit, Michigan Sat 24 Oct 2026 20.14 EDT First published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 19.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Barack Obama told a Detroit crowd on Saturday that Abdul El-Sayed was “fighting for change, real change, that will get money out of politics and put money in your pocket”, as he threw his weight behind the Democratic Senate candidate and the rest of the ticket on the first day of early voting in Michigan. Obama said in front of thousands of onlookers at Cass technical high school in Detroit that El-Sayed would “finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every single American”. The former president headlined the rally for El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate, and secretary of state Jocelyn Benson, the party’s candidate for governor, at an evening event to “get out the vote”. He accused Donald Trump of “enriching himself and his family”, and said the administration had set a “culture … at the top” of taking favors. “Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this,” he said. The rally came on the first day of Michigan’s early voting period, with the general election on 3 November. It was also Obama’s first weekend of in-person campaigning during the midterms, which started in Cleveland, Ohio, earlier in the day to stump for the former Ohio senator Sherrod Brown and Democratic nominee for governor Amy Acton earlier in the weekend. He issued similarly scathing remarks aimed at the White House and the GOP . View image in fullscreen Abdul El-Sayed speaks to supporters during a campaign rally in Detroit on Saturday. Photograph: Paul Sancya/AP The Detroit stop is Obama’s first public show of support for El-Sayed, who emerged from a bitter August primary in which the former president stayed on the sidelines. El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne county health official, beat the moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens who was riding on the backing of the Democratic establishment and pro-Israel organizations. Obama was on the offensive against the administration, mocking the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, as “laser-focused” on the “jawline and testosterone levels of our troops”, asking: “How much time do you think this man spends in front of the mirror every day?” On tariffs, Obama said Trump was toughest on “that well-known evil empire”, referring to Canada, a few minutes’ drive from Detroit across the bridge. “These are the people who gave us Martin Short and maple syrup,” he said. He even took a jab at Trump’s attempts to renovate the White House. “He should be on HGTV,” Obama said of the many renovations in Washington, including the White House ballroom and the Rose Garden. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Questions had hung over whether Obama would back El-Sayed at all. El-Sayed, a champion of Medicare for All, had at one point called the Affordable Care Act, Obama’s signature domestic achievement, an incremental fix. The two men spoke by phone after the primary, and El-Sayed has since called Obama a mentor figure. View image in fullscreen The rally for Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit on Saturday. Photograph: Paul Sancya/AP El-Sayed has the most ground to make up in Wayne county, where Detroit is the county seat, after Stevens beat him there by about 51% to 45% in the August primaries. Obama last campaigned in Detroit – which is more than three-quarters Black – in October 2024 for Kamala Harris, and Harris herself appeared with El-Sayed in Detroit last month. Republicans have not held a Michigan Senate seat in 25 years, but the party sees the seat as one of its better pickup chances nationwide. El-Sayed faces Mike Rogers, a former congressman endorsed by Donald Trump who lost a 2024 Senate matchup against Democratic senator Elissa Slotkin by less than half a percentage point. The Cook Political Report rates this race a toss-up. Slotkin, a featured speaker at the rally, told the crowd that “Michigan believes in electing fighters”. And when it came to any disagreements she may have with El-Sayed, she said: “It’s OK because we agree on so much more.” “We’re putting a check and balance on Donald Trump in the White House,” she said. A Marist poll of likely voters statewide conducted in mid-October put El-Sayed at 50% and Rogers at 48%, within the margin of error. RealClearPolitics’s average had El-Sayed ahead by about 2.6 points in a similar timeframe. View image in fullscreen Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters during the campaign rally in Detroit on Saturday. Photograph: Paul Sancya/AP Trump has attacked El-Sayed throughout the campaign, calling him a “jihadist”, pointing to his middle name and alleging that he had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which El-Sayed strongly denies, and has created one of the most viral moments of the year. El-Sayed has also faced a barrage of criticism from the establishment wing of the Democratic party over his appearances with leftwing streamer Hasan Piker . Trump is due in the state himself on Sunday, when he will hold a rally for Michigan Republicans in Port Huron, on the Canadian border. The city said it will be the first presidential visit to St Clair county. If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim and first Egyptian American in the US Senate. Benson faces the Republican congressman John James; a James win would make him Michigan’s first Black governor. Turning to the disagreements between them, Obama acknowledged that some people had pointed out that El-Sayed “didn’t like some things you did as president”. “We are not going to agree on every detail of every issue,” he said. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.” “We share those values of making sure everybody gets a fair shot in this society,” Obama said, “and that the system’s not just run for those at the top.” Explore more on these topics Michigan US midterm elections 2026 Barack Obama US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
